bib.title: Choice of Plausible Alternatives: An Evaluation of Commonsense Causal Reasoning
bib.venue: AAAI 2011 Spring Symposium on Logical Formalizations of Commonsense Reasoning (SS-11-06)

question: How can progress in open-domain commonsense causal reasoning be measured with a validated, automatically scored question set?
hypothesis: Simple associative corpus statistics will perform only moderately above chance while humans are near perfect, leaving a gap for future systems.
contributions: COPA: 1000 forced-choice commonsense causal questions with dev/test split
Authoring methodology for breadth, clarity and rater agreement

method.summary: Authors wrote 1000 premise plus two-alternative questions (cause or effect), validated by human raters, split 500/500 dev/test. Three unsupervised co-occurrence baselines using PMI and Dice are scored by accuracy.
method.task: Commonsense causal reasoning, forced choice between two alternatives (forward: effect; backward: cause)

datasets.name: COPA
datasets.source: Authored by the researchers; topics from 1M personal weblog stories (Aug-Sep 2008, Gordon & Swanson 2009) and Library of Congress Thesaurus for Graphic Materials subject terms; available at http://ict.usc.edu/~gordon/copa.html
datasets.preprocessing: Past tense, brief, no proper names or slang; order of questions and position of correct alternative randomised

datasets.name: Project Gutenberg
datasets.preprocessing: Content words only; co-occurrence within window W=5, 25 or 50

models.name: Gutenberg word-pair PMI/Dice
models.architecture: Unsupervised correlation score averaged over content word pairs

models.name: Web word-pair PMI/Dice
models.architecture: Same formula with search engine hit counts (Bing, Google, Yahoo)

models.name: Web phrase-level PMI/Dice
models.architecture: Whole premise and alternative as search query

inference.decoding: Select the alternative with the larger causality score
inference.samples: Single deterministic run per configuration; no seeds (unsupervised)
inference.retrieval: Search engine hit counts (Bing, Google, Yahoo); query date not stated

parameters.reverse_word_order: used for backward-causal questions since measures are asymmetric

metrics.name: accuracy
metrics.definition: fraction of questions where the higher-scoring alternative is the intended one

eval.protocol: Evaluated on dev, test and dev+test (unsupervised, so combined is valid); significance versus 50% at 0.05/0.01/0.001 (test type not stated). Human validation: 10 volunteers, 2 raters per question. No human accuracy figure is given, only kappa.

results.claim: Best baseline (Gutenberg PMI, W=5) reaches 58.3% on all 1000 questions, vs 50% random.
results.setup: Unsupervised PMI over Project Gutenberg co-occurrence, window W=5, dev+test 1000 questions
results.table: Table 1, row Dev + Test PMI, column W=5

results.claim: Best baseline on the 500-question test set is Gutenberg PMI W=5.
results.setup: PMI, window W=5, test set 500 questions; ** p<0.01 vs random
results.table: Table 1, row Test Set PMI, column W=5

results.claim: Same baseline on the 500-question dev set.
results.setup: PMI, W=5, dev set 500 questions; ** p<0.01
results.table: Table 1, row Dev Set PMI, column W=5

results.claim: Gutenberg Dice W=5 scores 56.0% on test.
results.table: Table 1, row Test Set Dice, column W=5

results.claim: Web phrase-level Dice with Bing reaches 57.8% on test.
results.setup: Whole premise and alternative as query, Bing hits, Dice, test 500; ** p<0.01
results.table: Table 1, row Test Set Dice, column Bing (web word phrase level)

results.claim: Web phrase-level Dice with Bing on dev+test.
results.table: Table 1, row Dev + Test Dice, column Bing (web word phrase level)

results.table: Table 1, row Test Set PMI, column Google (web word phrase level)

results.claim: Human raters agree almost perfectly on the intended answer.
results.setup: 10 volunteers, 200 questions each, 2 raters per question
results.quote: Agreement between authors was high (Cohen's Κ = 0.965).

results.claim: Volunteers disagreed with the author's intended answer on 26 questions, which were replaced.
results.setup: Replacements validated by two additional raters; 1000 final questions
results.quote: these volunteers answered 26 questions differently than was intended by the author of the question

results.claim: COPA has 1000 questions split equally into dev and test.
A random baseline scores exactly 50% because the correct position is randomised.
Smallest window is best, suggesting causally related events are described close together.
results.setup: Gutenberg PMI, W=5 vs W=25 (58.2) and W=50 (56.2) on dev+test
results.quote: suggesting that causally related events are typically described in close proximity to one another

limits: Only unsupervised associative baselines; no supervised or knowledge-based system tested
No human accuracy is reported, only inter-rater kappa 0.965
Significance test used is not named
Web hit-count baselines depend on unknown search engine mechanisms and date
Questions are single-author written, with the authors' own creative choices, 500 test items so small differences are noisy
Authors concede baselines are not expected to be competitive; best is 58.3%

terms.definition: Choice Of Plausible Alternatives: a premise and two plausible causes or effects, where the correct choice is the more plausible

lineage.note: COPA adapts the RTE question-set design (dev/test split, balanced)

lineage.work: Turney, Mining the Web for synonyms: PMI-IR versus LSA on TOEFL
Gordon & Swanson, Identifying Personal Stories in Millions of Weblog Entries
Gerber, Gordon & Sagae, Open-domain Commonsense Reasoning Using Discourse Relations from a Corpus of Weblog Stories

figures.caption: Three baseline results for the COPA evaluation. The results are computed in terms of accuracy and the ones marked with ***, **, and * are statistically significantly better at the 0.001, 0.01, and 0.05 levels, respectively, than the random baseline (50% accuracy).
figures.why: Shows all baseline accuracies by window and search engine against 50% chance
